name: Farr's Law
aliases: The law of epidemic rise and fall
statement: Epidemics tend to rise and fall in a roughly symmetric bell-shaped curve over time.
meaning: Farr's law is the empirical observation that epidemics tend to rise and fall over time in a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped pattern that can be approximated by a normal curve: the number of cases or deaths climbs to a peak and then declines in a broadly mirror-image fashion. William Farr, a pioneering British medical statistician, noted this regularity in 1840 while analysing deaths in a smallpox epidemic, showing that the rate of rise and decline followed a predictable mathematical pattern. It is a descriptive regularity rather than a mechanistic model, fitting a curve to observed data without explaining the underlying biology of transmission. As one of the earliest applications of mathematics to epidemics, it helped found the quantitative study of disease and has been revived to forecast the trajectory and peak of later epidemics.
mechanism: Farr observed that the counts of deaths in successive time periods during an epidemic did not rise and fall haphazardly but followed a regular pattern, with the ratios of successive counts declining in an orderly way, tracing out an approximately bell-shaped curve. He treated the epidemic's course as something whose laws of action could be determined by observation even if its cause was unknown, plotting mortality over time and fitting the regular pattern. The symmetry reflects the natural dynamics of a susceptible population being infected and then depleted, though Farr described the shape empirically rather than deriving it from transmission mechanics. Modern epidemiologists have used the same curve-fitting idea to project where an epidemic might peak, treating incidence as approximately normal in time.

examples.text: Farr derived the pattern in 1840 from deaths in a smallpox epidemic, showing quarterly deaths traced a roughly bell-shaped curve, one of the first mathematical treatments of an epidemic.
Bregman and Langmuir applied Farr's law in 1990 to project the AIDS epidemic's peak, but the epidemic kept growing, exposing the law's limits as a forecasting tool.
Farr worked at the General Register Office and, alongside John Snow, is regarded as a founder of epidemiology and the statistical study of mortality.

variants.name: Brownlee's revival
variants.text: The early twentieth-century elaboration of Farr's pattern by John Brownlee, who helped solidify it as a named law of epidemic curves.

variants.name: Modern curve-fitting forecasts
variants.text: Later uses of the law to project the peak and trajectory of epidemics such as AIDS, drug-overdose mortality, and discussions during COVID-19.

whyItMatters: Farr's law is an early landmark in applying mathematics and statistics to epidemics, part of the nineteenth-century birth of epidemiology and vital statistics in which Farr, working alongside John Snow, was a central figure. Its bell-shaped description of how epidemics rise and fall offers an intuitive picture of an outbreak's course and has been revived repeatedly to attempt forecasts of where an epidemic will peak. Yet its mixed record as a predictor also makes it a cautionary example, showing the difference between describing a pattern and understanding the mechanism that generates it, a distinction central to modern epidemic modelling.

working.text: expect an epidemic's cases to rise to a peak and fall away in a roughly symmetric, bell-shaped pattern over time.
use the regularity descriptively, fitting a curve to counts of cases or deaths rather than modelling transmission mechanics.
treat projections from the law cautiously, since real epidemics can break the symmetry through waves, interventions, and new variants.

limits: Farr's law is an empirical regularity, not a guaranteed law or a mechanistic model, so real epidemics can deviate sharply from the symmetric bell shape. Multiple waves, public-health interventions, behavioural change, and new variants can all break the symmetry, as the failed 1990 projection of the AIDS epidemic showed when the outbreak kept growing instead of cresting. It describes a tendency in the data without explaining the biology of transmission, so it offers no causal understanding and its forecasts are only as good as the assumption that the curve will stay symmetric, which often fails. It is best seen as a descriptive pattern, not a predictive rule.
misreadings: Farr's law is descriptive, not mechanistic; it fits a curve to epidemic data without explaining why the pattern arises, so it is not a model of transmission. It is a tendency, not a certainty: real epidemics can and do depart from the symmetric bell shape, producing multiple waves or sustained growth, so using it to guarantee a peak has repeatedly failed. And the name credits Farr's 1840 observation, but the law was elaborated and solidified later, notably by Brownlee, so it reflects a lineage of work rather than a single fixed derivation.
origin: Formulated by the British medical statistician William Farr in 1840 from his analysis of a smallpox epidemic while at the General Register Office, and later revived by John Brownlee and applied to modern epidemic forecasting.
